extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, statesmen, and scholars of governance
extracted.subtask_description: Examination of causes of corruption, mechanisms of preservation, and characteristic differences among monarchies, tyrannies, oligarchies, and democracies, with practical examples and prescriptions for rulers. Emphasises what produces stability or revolution in different regime-types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kingdom vs. Tyranny (definition/distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A kingdom is formed to protect the better sort of people and kings are appointed from those chosen for superior virtue, noble descent, or beneficent actions; a tyrant is chosen out of the meanest populace and is an enemy to the better sort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle treats a tyranny as the worst government because it partakes of the defects of both oligarchy and democracy. Examples given: Phidon at Argos, Phalaris in Ionia, Pisistratus at Athens (origins of tyrannies may be demagogues, over-mighty kings, or life-appointed officers who centralize power).

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of Tyranny (mechanisms of establishment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tyrannies arise by demagogy, kings exceeding lawful power, or powerful officers (appointed for life) placing supreme power in one person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete mechanisms: demagogues gaining popular support by oppressing nobles; kings extending their power beyond legal bounds; officers of civil and religious affairs leveraging their position. Examples: Cypselus, Pisistratus, Dionysius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyranny mirrors oligarchy and democracy (characteristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tyranny contains what is bad in both democracy and oligarchy: from oligarchy it seeks gain and distrusts the people; from democracy it quarrels with and destroys nobles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shared behaviours include depriving the populace of arms, persecuting or exiling rivals, using fear and poverty to control citizens, and persecuting the wealthy or honorable as impediments to power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of Conspiracy/Overthrow (hatred, contempt, fear, loss of property)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conspiracies against rulers arise chiefly from hatred (revenge), contempt (for the ruler's person or life-style), fear (of punishment), and deprivation of private fortunes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: plots motivated by personal insult (Harmodius/Aristogiton), resentment of corporal punishment or public indignity, fear of punishment (Artabanes), and loss of property provoking rebellion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal affronts and revenge as catalysts for assassination
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidents of personal insult or injury (to self or family) often provoke conspiracies and assassination rather than cold ambition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative cases: the killing related to Harmodius's sister; Periander and Thrasybulus; Pausanias killing Philip after an insult. Revenge can unite many against a ruler even without aims for personal advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear as a cause of conspiracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear of punishment or retribution can motivate conspirators, especially when those involved anticipate severe consequences from the ruler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Artabanes conspired against Xerxes through fear of punishment. Fear operates alongside other motives and often combines with contempt or hatred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambitious military leaders as likely revolutionaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Those with military honours and bold dispositions are most likely to engage in sedition, because strength and courage together make them predisposed to attempt revolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Generals like Cyrus (against Astyages), Suthes against Amadocus. Such leaders often despise weak rulers and seize opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: External opposition and principle-based rivalry cause overthrow
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposition from neighbouring states or states of contrary principle (e.g., democracies against tyrannies) often contributes to the overthrow of tyrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Lacedaemonians destroying many tyrannies; Syracusans acting internally and externally. External pressure interacts with internal instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability of kingdoms depends on moderation of the king's power
rubrics_metrics.description: The less extensive a king's power is kept, the longer and more stable his government will be; limiting power preserves submission by keeping the ruler near an equality of condition with subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Molossi and Sparta (division of power; Theopompus' ephori made the kingdom longer-lasting). Principle: reduce potential causes of envy and contempt by not over-centralizing authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyrannical preservation method A: suppress mutual confidence and resources
rubrics_metrics.description: One way tyrants preserve power is by keeping citizens poor, isolated, uneducated, and mutually distrustful so they lack the means and will to conspire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tactics: forbid public meals/clubs/education, employ spies and 'listeners', station foreigners near gates, use foreign guards, multiply taxes, confiscate private property, engage people in war to occupy them, reward slaves and women to report secrets, prevent formation of mutual confidence. Examples: Persians, practices attributed to Periander and Dionysius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyrannical preservation method B: appear kingly and secure submission
rubrics_metrics.description: The opposite preservation tactic is to make the tyranny appear kingly—secure absolute power but govern with appearances of legitimacy and public concern so even the unwilling submit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behaviours to adopt: appear attentive to public affairs, manage finances transparently, avoid ostentatious profusion, be respectable not despised, moderate personal pleasures or feign moderation, adorn the city, be observant of religion, respect men of merit, let honours flow from oneself while censures come from subordinates, avoid making any subordinate too great, and avoid corporal punishment or public disgrace. This makes the tyrant seem a guardian rather than a plunderer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three objects/ends tyrants aim to secure
rubrics_metrics.description: Tyrants aim that their citizens (1) be poor and abject, (2) have no confidence in one another, and (3) be totally without means/power to act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All tyrannical policies tend toward these three ends because without poverty, distrust, or powerlessness, conspiracies and revolutions become possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid corporal punishment and public disgrace of honourable men
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical punishment or public indignity of those with a delicate sense of honour provokes resentment; such punishments should be avoided or administered in a paternal, not contemptuous, manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If punishment must be used, it should resemble a father's correction and be followed by greater honours to compensate; humiliation incites plots from those who value honour more than life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of foreigners and flattery for tyrannical security
rubrics_metrics.description: Tyrants should rely on foreign guards and flatterers rather than trusting citizens of merit, and prefer strangers in intimacy because citizens may conspire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flatterers and servile attendants are prized by tyrants; citizens of worth are seen as threats. Examples: tyrants often surround themselves with the worst characters and foreigners at table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political appearance: associate nobles and soothe the people (middle-rank posture)
rubrics_metrics.description: To preserve a regime (especially monarchy), a ruler should affect a middle rank, associate nobles with himself, soothe public opinion, and appear as guardian rather than superior despot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing one's life and manners to be at least partly virtuous and making the government honourable increases durability and imitability; distributing honours and respecting men of merit prevents envy and sedition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation, obedience to laws, and popularity lengthen tyrannies
rubrics_metrics.description: When tyrants or rulers use power with moderation, obey laws in many particulars, and govern without visible reliance on guards, their rule lasts longer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Orthagoras at Sicyon (moderation & obedience), Cypselus at Corinth (popularity, governing without guards), Pisistratus submitting to courts at Athens in some instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundation of a democratic state: liberty and equality by numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: The foundation of democracy is liberty, conceived as the ability to govern and be governed alternately; equality in democracy measures by numbers (majority) rather than by worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: in democracy the poor (being the greater number) ought to have more power than the rich; liberty includes living 'as every one likes' and being under command only by rotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of governmental change and critique of single-cause explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments change for many reasons (poverty, insults, shifts in fortune, differing social composition) and it is erroneous to assign a single universal cause (e.g., Plato's focus on luxury causing democracy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle argues changes do not follow a fixed circle necessarily; examples show tyrannies change into various other regimes and that social composition (occupations, wealth distribution, insults, loss of honours) matters for regime change.
